title: BWF World Championships Return to Delhi After 17 Years as India Targets Home Glory
excerpt: After venue controversy at the India Open, organisers have overhauled conditions at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium for badminton's flagship event, August 17-23.
body:
• The BWF World Championships return to India for the first time in 17 years, running August 17-23 at New Delhi's Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium.
  • Organisers have overhauled venue conditions after the India Open controversy in January, when bird droppings, stray animals, and poor air quality drew fierce criticism from international players.
  • India's badminton programme has earned 15 World Championship medals since 1983, led by PV Sindhu's five medals including a historic gold in 2019.
  • Defending men's champion Shi Yu Qi and women's titleholder Akane Yamaguchi headline the field, with Sindhu spearheading India's challenge on home soil.

The BWF World Championships arrive in New Delhi on August 17, marking the first time India has hosted badminton's flagship event since Hyderabad staged it in 2009. The 30th edition of the tournament will run through August 23 at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium, with the draw announced this week.

From Embarrassment to Redemption

The build-up has been defined by a single question: can Delhi deliver? The January India Open at the same venue became a global embarrassment after Singapore's Loh Kean Yew said he struggled to breathe and wore a mask outside his hotel room. Denmark's Mia Blichfeldt described conditions as "dirty and unhealthy," citing bird droppings on courts, dust-filled air, and inadequate heating.

"I breathe less. I just wear my mask when I can. Everyone's stamina just dropped two levels."

— Loh Kean Yew, 2021 World Champion

Loh's match against India's HS Prannoy was halted twice after birds fouled the court. Thailand's Ratchanok Intanon complained about cold conditions, and South Korea's Kang Minhyuk posted footage of a monkey inside the training venue. World No. 3 Anders Antonsen skipped the tournament entirely, blaming Delhi's air pollution.

Organisers Promise a Different Show

BWF Secretary General Thomas Lund told Reuters that the Badminton Association of India acted swiftly after the India Open to address venue cleanliness and environmental conditions. August's monsoon weather typically brings significantly better air quality than January's notorious smog season, removing one major concern.

BAI general secretary Sanjay Mishra said organisers had strengthened animal-control measures with a triple-door entry system, round-the-clock security, sealed access points, and coordination with local authorities to relocate stray animals. The venue roof has been inspected and waterproofed, the air-conditioning system tested, and lighting upgraded.

"We are confident that the event will offer nothing less than a seamless, world-class spectacle for players, officials and fans alike."

— Sanjay Mishra, BAI General Secretary

India's 17-Year Transformation

When Hyderabad last hosted in 2009, Indian badminton largely revolved around one name — Saina Nehwal. Olympic medals were a dream, world titles seemed distant, and a 14-year-old PV Sindhu was quietly training at the Pullela Gopichand academy in Hyderabad.

The breakthrough came in 2011 when Jwala Gutta and Ashwini Ponnappa won women's doubles bronze at the World Championships, ending India's 28-year medal drought at the event. Saina followed with a silver in 2015, becoming India's first World No. 1 in women's singles. Then Sindhu elevated Indian badminton to another level, accumulating five World Championship medals and winning gold in Basel in 2019 — India's first world title.

The country's medal streak at the Worlds has continued unbroken since 2011, most recently extended by Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty's bronze in Paris 2025. India now has 15 podium finishes at the World Championships since Prakash Padukone's bronze in Copenhagen in 1983.

The Field and India's Medal Hopes

China's defending men's singles champion Shi Yu Qi and Japan's women's titleholder Akane Yamaguchi lead the international entries. Sindhu, a twice Olympic medallist, will spearhead India's challenge in women's singles on home soil. Rankireddy and Shetty will look to build on their doubles momentum.

For Indian badminton, Delhi 2026 is more than a tournament — it is a celebration of a remarkable journey from one name and zero medals to a programme that consistently challenges the sport's traditional Asian powerhouses on the world stage.
